svg.font-family: Inter, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: Figure 1. What each relay knows, and why that is a structure rather than a promise
svg.desc: A chain showing five parties: you, the guard relay, the middle relay, the exit relay, and the destination. The guard knows your address and the middle relay it hands to, but not your destination. The middle relay knows only the two relays either side of it, and neither end. The exit relay knows the destination and the middle relay, but not your address. The destination sees the exit relay's address. A band below states the resulting property: no single party holds both your address and your destination, and this holds because of how the circuit is built rather than because anybody promised it. A comparison table contrasts this with a single tunnel provider, who holds both halves and is prevented from acting on them only by policy, and with a chain of two providers, where the separation exists but you chose both parties and they are commercial entities that can merge. A closing band notes that the middle relay exists to stop the guard and the exit from ever speaking to each other directly.
svg.text: Figure 1: What Each Relay Knows, and Why It Is a Structure
The usual diagram shows three hops. The useful part is the column nobody draws: what would have to happen for one party to link you to where you went.
YOU
and your network operator
GUARD
your first hop, and Figure 2
MIDDLE
the one with a real job
EXIT
carries your traffic in clear
DESTINATION
sees the exit, not you

g.text: Does not know: where you went

svg.text: The property, stated exactly
No single party holds both your address and your destination. That is not a promise anybody made and it is not a policy that could be revised. It follows
from how the circuit is constructed: each relay is handed only the address of the next one, and the layers are encrypted so that no relay can read past its own.
You do not have to trust any relay for this to hold. You have to trust that they are not all the same party, which is a different and much weaker requirement.
COMPARE WITH MODULE 6 SO FAR
WHO HOLDS BOTH HALVES
WHAT STOPS THEM USING IT
One tunnel provider, Lesson 6.1
the arrangement most people run
The provider. Both halves, continuously.
Their policy, which Lesson 6.3 established
you cannot verify.
Two providers chained, Lesson 6.4
the arrangement people build by hand
Neither, by design. But you selected both,
and companies merge.
Corporate separation, which is a
commercial fact rather than a technical one.
A Tor circuit, this lesson
relays picked by your client, not by you
Nobody. And the relays are strangers who
did not choose each other.
The construction itself, plus the fact that
a fresh circuit picks a different three.
Why the middle relay is there at all
It looks like a spare part. It is not. Without it the guard and
the exit would connect to each other directly, and each would
learn the other's address for your circuit.
The middle exists so that the two relays which each know
half of the answer never speak to each other.
Why not four hops, or ten
More hops cost latency and network capacity and buy nothing
against the adversary that matters, who watches both ends and
wins regardless of what happens in the middle.
A non-standard path length also makes you rarer, and being
rare is the opposite of what you came here for.
This is why Tor is not a tunnel with extra hops. A tunnel asks you to trust one party. A circuit is built so that no party is in a position to be trusted.
Figure 3 is honest about where that argument gets weaker in practice, because it does get weaker.
